questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have always been very interested in the situation in Palestine and Israel and in the Middle East in general. I wanted to study abroad there in order to experience an every day life. On a more practical level, it was crucial for me to pick a destination, where KU had a collaboration and exchange agreement, and Hebrew University in Jerusalem was the only partner university in the Middle East. I would never have managed to plan and sort everything out otherwise.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall I am very happy that I went. It gave me experiences that I will carry with me for the rest of my life. Everyday was not funny - it was also tough, and there were days of feeling homesick or frustrated with a new set of University bureaucracy.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was easy enough. I little bit complicated by office hours and weekends, though.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not get a lot of informtation, but I also missed an introduction because of my travel plan. My first month was a pre-semester programme, and the information in that regard was pretty scarce. We did not really know what was expected from us, and often our professor texted us the night before when we had classes in the following day or week.

Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
First, I moved into a so called student village - 10 blocks with hundreds of students living in small appartments. However, I did not really like that. I was in a five person-appartment with two rommates, who both moved out during the first two weeks. I could not get any information about whether or not anyone else would move in. In addition, the appartments were empty (except from beds, tables and chairs), so it would have been quite expencive to buy pots, pans, cuddlery, plates - everything, actually (not to mention teh fact that the rent was also crazily expensive). Furthermore, I came there to be a part of another culture. I did not whish to live in a dorm outside of the city centre with a fence around with students as my only neighbours. 
Eventually I found a room with two german exchange students in the city centre, and that was great! But I would not have been able to find something like that from home, since I only heard about it through classmates. Therefore, the Student Village can be a good place to start, and then it is always possible to seach for something else from there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In the case of Jerusalem, you can easily find something that is cheaper than the Student Village - even though you have to pay for public transportation. The busses and trams are working very well, so it is no problem to live off campus.

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it a bit difficult, since there are some different programs, where you can find courses. This meant that there were different requirments and registration processes. Furthermore, the deadlines at KU and HUJI were not in sync, which occasionally ment doubble work.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to register for a pre semester programme before arrival, but the other classes I had to register for when the semester began. There was one "shopping week" where we could go to different classes before deciding. Then we had to apply for classes and talk with a counselor. As I mentioned, there were some different programs with different application processes. This was a bit tricky, and sometimes I felt trapped between requirments from KU and HUJI. It all worked out, though. But I could have done without the stress of figuring this out in the first 1,5 month.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A student counselor and mail assistance.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Seccessful. I managed to get them all. I had some mandatory classes that I had to take in order to live up to the requirments from KU. This made things more difficult, but it worked out.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even though you can read somewhere that you don't meet the requirments for a course that you want, try anyway. There are a lot (!!) of rules at HUJI, but sometimes they can be bend a little.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I fond that the courses differed quite a lot on what you might call the narrative about the conflict/occupation. Some courses were so biased that I found it to be a bit problematic.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the BA courses to be quite a lot easier than what I am used to, but the MA-classes were the same or maybe a bit more difficult than my home university.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It sometimes seemed a bit more... Old fashioned. Not understood in the sense that the professor did all the talking. More in the sense that they would ask random random people in the class about homework, translations or something like that. I also has amazing professors who would engage the class in a safe and nice way.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: One City - Many Religions (pre-semester), The Battle over the Bibel - the Bible in the eyes of the Muslin, Jews and Christians, Belief and Ritual in Islam, Keys to the modern Middle East, The Conquest Narrative - Joshua 1-12, Biblical Hebrew, The Making of the Bible.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The Battle over the Bible was super interesting if you are interested in the abrahamic religions. 
Belief and Rutual in Islam was really great! It was on an introductury level. 
Keys to the Modern Middle East was also a great introduction.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Jerusalem is expensive! If you live in the dorms, you have to pay everything in advance and buy everything for the kitchen.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food, coffee and other drinks were (at least in West Jerusalem) more expensive. In East (and in the other palestinian aeras in general), it is cheaper. Transportation is also very cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not use it too much. In the beginning I went on a few trips which was good.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not sure, but I think there were religious and political clubs as well as planned activities for international students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Some of the stuff planned by Rothberg (the international faculty).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the west bank. We were recomended not to, which I fould quite provocative. Bethlehem is great and very close. The dead sea is a must, and there are some beautiful hikes there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: In the beginning, I sometimes felt a bit unsafe as a young women, since cars would honk and men approach me. But it got better, and people were super nice and hospitable.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The international students are isolated in their own faculty, which is a bit of a shame.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The constant and visible military precense and security meassurements! And also just living in the middle of a conflict so toxic and with such an intense battle over information and truth.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The hospitality!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to push for what you want. Don't worry if people behind desks seem impolite. And be critical of the conflict narrative no matter what version of the story, you hear.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: no

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Just having a normal everyday life there. It was really great!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Living in the middle of the conflict. Worrying about what to say in which crowds. Thinking about whether you should say thank you in hebrew or arabic in the different coffee shops.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: no

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
